item.title: Fukushuji Temple, Iwakuni — Guide
item.description: Fukushuji is a quiet, atmospheric temple set in the wooded hills of Iwakuni in eastern Yamaguchi, a gentle counterpoint to the crowds at the famous Kintaikyo Bridge not far away. Temples like this one reward the traveller willing to step slightly off the main route: mossy stone steps and lanterns, a modest main hall among old trees, and grounds that turn fresh green in early summer and glow with maple colour in autumn.

item.title: Gunkei Temple, Hitoyoshi — Guide
item.description: In the castle town of Hitoyoshi, deep in the mountains of southern Kumamoto along the Kuma River, Gunkei Temple offers a quiet and historic stop amid the valley’s rich cultural heritage. Hitoyoshi flourished for centuries as the seat of the Sagara clan, who ruled the isolated Kuma region for some 700 years, and the town preserves an unusual concentration of old temples, shrines and cultural sites — including nationally important treasures — reflecting a distinctive local Buddhist and Shinto culture.

item.title: Kiyomizu Temple, Kumamoto — Guide
item.description: Kiyomizu Temple in Kumamoto is a peaceful Buddhist temple offering a tranquil retreat from the busier city sights. Set among greenery, its weathered wooden halls, mossy stone steps, statues and quiet grounds create a serene, contemplative atmosphere that changes gently with the seasons — cherry or plum blossom in spring, fresh green in summer, and coloured leaves in autumn. Away from the tourist crowds of the castle, it’s the kind of local temple where you can slow down, stroll the grounds, offer a prayer, and enjoy the timeless calm of a working place of worship.

item.title: Kosanji Temple and the Hill of Hope — Guide
item.description: Kosanji is one of the most extraordinary and flamboyant temples in Japan, built in the twentieth century by a businessman in memory of his mother. Spread across a hillside on Ikuchijima island along the Shimanami Kaido, its buildings are lavish recreations of famous temple architecture from across Japan, painted in dazzling colours and gold, alongside a vast underground ‘cave of hell and heaven’. Crowning it all is the Hill of Hope (Miraishin no Oka), a surreal hilltop entirely sculpted from gleaming white Italian marble into abstract terraces, arches and viewpoints overlooking the Seto Inland Sea.

item.title: Myozen-ji Temple — Guide
item.description: Myozen-ji is a historic Buddhist temple in Kumamoto, offering a calm and atmospheric stop away from the main tourist trail. Its aged wooden main hall, temple gate, statues and gardens carry the quiet dignity of a long-established place of worship, and the grounds change with the seasons — blossom in spring, cool green in summer, and coloured foliage in autumn. Like many of Kumamoto’s neighbourhood temples, it invites visitors to slow down, wander the peaceful precincts, admire the traditional architecture and enjoy a moment of stillness.

item.title: Nanzoin Temple: The Giant Reclining Buddha — Guide
item.description: Nanzoin Temple, tucked into the wooded hills of Sasaguri just east of Fukuoka, is famous for its colossal reclining Buddha (Nehanzo), one of the largest bronze statues in the world. Depicting the Buddha at the moment of entering nirvana, the statue is around 41 metres long and 11 metres high — bigger than the Statue of Liberty is tall — and weighs some 300 tonnes. Reached through peaceful temple grounds dotted with smaller statues, stone Buddhas and forest paths, the giant figure is a genuinely awe-inspiring sight.

item.title: Sanjusangendo: The Hall of 1,001 Kannon — Guide
item.description: Sanjusangendo is one of Kyoto’s most quietly overwhelming sights: a long, narrow wooden hall, at 120 metres the longest in Japan, filled with a thousand and one statues of Kannon, the Buddhist deity of compassion. Rank upon rank of gilded, thousand-armed figures stand in tiered rows to either side of a great seated central Kannon, each face subtly different, backed by twenty-eight guardian deities and the thunder and wind gods carved with astonishing dynamism.

item.title: Seiryuji Temple & Its Giant Daibutsu — Guide
item.description: Seiryuji sits on the wooded slopes of western Hiroshima, well away from the tourist trail, and its landmark is a huge bronze Daibutsu, a Great Buddha seated serenely on the hillside and gazing out over the city and the delta below. The temple grounds climb the slope through halls, statuary and quiet corners, with views that open up as you ascend, and the whole place sees a fraction of the visitors of the central sights.

item.title: Shitennoji: Japan's Oldest Official Temple — Guide
item.description: Shitennoji claims to be the oldest officially administered temple in Japan, founded in 593 by Prince Shotoku, the statesman who did more than anyone to establish Buddhism in the country. Fires and war have destroyed its buildings many times, but each rebuilding has faithfully followed the original sixth-century plan: a rigidly symmetrical line of inner gate, five-storey pagoda and golden hall enclosed by a cloister, the earliest temple layout in Japan.

item.title: Zen Meditation in Kyoto: A Zazen Experience — Guide
item.description: As the historic centre of Rinzai Zen, Kyoto is the best place in Japan to try zazen, the seated meditation at the heart of Zen practice. A number of temples run sessions open to visitors, some in English, in which a monk guides you in the posture, breathing and stillness of zazen in a quiet hall, often followed by a short dharma talk and a bowl of tea. In the traditional style, an attendant may walk the hall with the keisaku, a flat wooden stick used to strike the shoulders — not as punishment but, on request, to restore focus.

item.title: Zojo-ji Temple — Guide
item.description: Zojo-ji, at the foot of Tokyo Tower in Shiba-koen, is one of Tokyo’s most important and historic temples, with a striking juxtaposition of old and new. Founded in the fourteenth century and later chosen as the family temple of the ruling Tokugawa shogunate, it was once an enormous temple complex, and several shoguns are buried in its mausoleum. Its imposing main gate, the Sangedatsumon, dates from 1622 and is one of the oldest wooden structures in Tokyo, having survived wars and disasters.

item.title: Showa Daibutsu (Seiryuji): Japan's Tallest Bronze Buddha — Guide
item.description: Just outside Aomori City, the tranquil temple of Seiryuji is home to the Showa Daibutsu — at 21.35 metres, Japan’s tallest seated bronze Great Buddha, taller even than the famous Buddhas of Nara and Kamakura. Cast in 1984, it presides over spacious grounds with a striking five-story pagoda. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aomori City, Aomori Hours ~9:00–17:30 (seasonal) Admission Around ¥500 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Year-round; autumn colours fine What to See The 21 m bronze Great Buddha, Japan’s tallest seated bronze figure.

item.title: Kinkaku-ji Guide: Kyoto's Golden Pavilion
item.description: A three-storey pavilion covered in pure gold leaf, mirrored perfectly in the still pond before it, framed by pines and — if you’re lucky — dusted with snow or backed by autumn maples: Kinkaku-ji is the postcard image of Kyoto, and one of the few sights that genuinely lives up to it. The Golden Pavilion shimmers whether under bright sun, soft cloud, or a rare winter snowfall, and the moment you round the path and it appears across the water is unforgettable.

item.title: Kiyomizu-dera Guide: The Temple on Stilts Above Kyoto
item.description: Perched on the wooded slopes of Higashiyama, Kiyomizu-dera juts out over the hillside on a vast wooden stage held up by enormous pillars — built, famously, without a single nail. From the stage you look out over a sea of maple and cherry trees to the rooftops of Kyoto beyond. It is one of Japan’s most beloved temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the climax of the most atmospheric temple approach in the city: the stone-paved, shop-lined slopes of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka.

item.title: Mount Oyama Guide: Cable Car, Afuri Shrine & Access
item.description: Rising at the eastern edge of the Tanzawa range, Mount Oyama (1,252 m) has been a place of worship and pilgrimage for centuries — and today it’s one of the most accessible and rewarding half-day mountains near Tokyo. A nostalgic shopping street of tofu restaurants and inns leads to a cable car that climbs to Afuri Shrine, with sweeping views over the Kanto Plain and, on clear days, the sea and Mt.

item.title: Narita-san Shinshoji Temple Guide: Access from the Airport & Tips
item.description: Just minutes from Narita Airport, Narita-san Shinshoji Temple is one of the most important and atmospheric Buddhist temples in the Tokyo area — the perfect first or last stop on a trip to Japan. Founded in 940 and headquarters of the Shingon Chisan sect, it enshrines Fudo Myo-o, the fierce, flame-wreathed guardian deity, and draws millions of worshippers a year (it ranks among Japan’s busiest for New Year’s visits). Spread across a hillside of grand halls, a soaring pagoda and a tranquil landscaped park, and approached by a charming old street of eel restaurants and souvenir shops, it offers a deep dose of living Japanese tradition right by the airport.

item.title: Senso-ji Temple Guide: Asakusa's Ancient Heart from Dawn to Dusk
item.description: Senso-ji is the oldest and most visited temple in Tokyo — but it is also one of the most misunderstood. Millions of visitors pass through the Kaminarimon gate, photograph the giant paper lantern, browse a few stalls on Nakamise-dori, and leave in 20 minutes. Those who stay longer, arrive earlier, or return in the evening discover something different entirely: a living place of worship with 1,400 years of continuous practice, where the incense smoke carries real prayers, and where the early morning light through the five-storey pagoda is among the most beautiful sights in the city.
